input: Given question: Poor James, a 5 year old boy, is brought to the GP by his mum who is concerned that he always seems more out of breath than the other children during sport and is often wheezy. You decide that the most likely diagnosis is asthma and prescribe Salbutamol. Which of the following best describes the mechanism of action of salbutamol? Option A: Beta-2-adrenoreceptor agonist Binds to beta-2-adrenoreceptors which are GPCRThis up regulates adenylate cyclasecAMP increases and activates protein kinase APKA switches of myosin light chain kinase Bronchial smooth muscle relaxes Option B: M3 receptor antagonist Binds to M3 which is a GPCR and blocks acetylcholine from binding This decreases cGMP production cGMP usually causes bronchial smooth muscle contractionLess cGMP causes bronchial smooth muscle relaxation Option C: M3 receptor agonist Binds to M3 which is a GPCR and blocks acetylcholine from bindingThis decreases cGMP productioncGMP usually causes bronchial smooth muscle contractionLess cGMP causes bronchial smooth muscle relaxation Option D: Beta-2-adrenoreceptor antagonistBinds to beta-2-adrenoreceptors which are GPCRThis up regulates adenylate cyclasecAMP increases and activates protein kinase APKA switches of myosin light chain kinaseBronchial smooth muscle relaxes Option E: Inhaled corticosteroid Binds to a glucocorticoid receptor Up regulates transcription anti-inflammatory mediatorsDown regulates transcription of inflammatory mediators Reduces inflammation The correct answer is Option A.
reference: The correct answer is A  Salbutamol is a sympathomimetic drug aka it mimics the sympathetic system effects. input: Given question: Colin the cell is still on his quest to have a family. The production of his protein has now entered into the translation phase. Every protein starts with a methionine amino acid. The codon that codes for this is AUG. What anticodon would the complementary tRNA molecule possess? Option A: TAC Option B: GCA Option C: CGU Option D: CGT Option E: UAC The correct answer is Option E.
reference: 3 bases code for the first amino acid and these 3 bases on mRNA are paired with the tRNA molecule. The order of these 3 bases determines the 2nd and 3rd bases of the coding strand which will then determine the amino acid. Remember the genetic code is degenerate so there can be multiple codons that code for the same amino acid. The synonymous codons are shown in the options above. The most common/typical codon is AUG as it is the first codon in the mRNA and also the start of the translation phase. It's worth noting that some proteins have "start" or "stop" signals which may be different from the usual AUG start. This is because the DNA coding strand was read by ribosomes in 3 base pairs so the end of one frame (15 base pairs) and the start of the next would be coded for by the same set of 3 bases. Therefore the 2nd and 3rd base pairs of the coding strand may not always code for the next amino acid in the sequence.
best_explanation:
Colin the cell is still on his quest to have a family. The production of his protein has now entered into the translation phase. Every protein starts with a methionine amino acid. The codon that codes for this is AUG. The anticodon that the complementary tRNA molecule would possess is UAC.

Explanation:

In the process of protein synthesis, the production of a protein starts with the transcription phase, where the genetic information in the DNA is used to create a complementary RNA molecule. This RNA molecule, called messenger RNA (mRNA), then travels to the cytoplasm where it is translated into a protein. The process of translation is initiated by the binding of the small ribosomal subunit to the mRNA and the first codon, which is typically AUG.

The complementary tRNA molecule that binds to the codon AUG is UAC. This is because the anticodon of tRNA molecule is complementary to the codon it binds to. The methionine amino acid is then added to the growing protein chain, and the process of translation continues until the stop codon is reached.

Therefore, the correct answer is Option E, UAC.

input: Given question: Joints have a rich nerve supply provided by articular nerves. Hilton's law states that the nerves supplying a joint also supply the muscles moving the joint and the skin covering their distal attachments. The nerve of a joint transmits impulses which play a key role in which sense? Option A: Nociception Option B: Proprioception Option C: Exteroception Option D: Interoception Option E: Kinesthesia The correct answer is Option B.
reference:
Hilton’s Law states that the nerves supplying a joint also supply the muscles moving the joint and the skin covering their distal attachments. This means that the nerve of a joint transmits impulses which are related to proprioception. Proprioception is the sense of where your body is in space and time. It allows you to close your eyes and still move your limbs without bumping into things. It is mediated by articular nerves.  Nociception is the sensation of pain. It is mediated by A-delta fibres which are slow (10-20m/s) conducting fibres. They transmit signals of intense pain, often from damaged tissues.  Exteroception is the sensory system concerned with our awareness of stimuli in the environment, such as light touch, vibration, pressure etc. It is mediated by free nerve endings, which are found in the skin.  Interoception refers to the conscious perception of physiological responses or bodily feelings, such as hunger, thirst, fatigue or discomfort. It is not well understood, but it may involve afferent neurons that do not synapse in the spinal cord, but rather in the brain stem or higher brain regions.  Kinesthesia refers to the awareness of the movement of your own body. It is proprioception over longer periods, and so includes the ability to learn and remember motor skills.  For more information on this topic see the PCS unit 3 tutorial on ‘General sensation: what comes in via the special senses?’  Case 6: ‘The cutaneous sensations of the upper limb’, in ‘Clinical Skills for Lower Limb and Trunk Injuries’, will allow you to develop your skills in examining patients with SBS. Joints have a rich nerve supply provided by articular nerves, which transmit impulses to the central nervous system, allowing us to sense the position, movement, and tension of the joints. reference:
Periaqueductal gray (PAG) is the primary control centre for descending pain modulation.The PAG sends descending projections to the dorsal horn and is the final pathway for the modulation of nociceptive sensory information. The PAG can inhibit or facilitate the release of substance P via interneurons that project to the dorsal horn. In this way it can influence the experience of pain.The dorsal horn of the spinal cord is where ascending sensory information from the body's tissues is processed and then sent to the brain for interpretation.The thalamus is the second relay station in the ascending pathways, receiving information from the dorsal horn and transmitting it to the somatosensory homunculus in the cerebral cortex.This information is then interpreted by the brain to determine the quality of the sensation, such as sharp/dull, aching etc.The nucleus raphe magnus is a part of the brainstem involved in the regulation of serotonin.Serotonin is important in the descending pain modulation system as it is a neurotransmitter used by the descending neurones projecting to the dorsal horn.  The reticular formation is a part of the brainstem involved in arousal and consciousness. It is not directly involved in pain modulation. information source; pain management lecture, PCS2 tutorial document, pain and nociception lecture, PCS1 tutorial document. references; McBeth, J. (2013). Pain and Nociception. In M. G. Sweeney (Ed.), The Neurology of Consciousness: Cognitive Neuroscience and Neuropathology (pp. 475-492). Academic Press. Dr Watson, PCS2 tutorial, descending pain modulation slide. Dr Watson, PCS1 tutorial, pain and nociception slide.

Explanation: The primary control centre for descending pain modulation is the periaqueductal gray (PAG). The PAG is a region in the midbrain that is involved in the regulation of pain, fear and other emotional responses. It is a key structure in the descending pain modulation pathway, which helps to inhibit or reduce pain signals as they travel from the spinal cord to the brain. The PAG receives inputs from several brain regions, including the rostral ventromedial medulla (RVM), dorsal horn of the spinal cord, and the hypothalamus, and sends descending projections to the dorsal horn of the spinal cord and other regions involved in pain modulation.

The thalamus is a subcortical structure involved in sensory processing and relaying of information to the cortex, but it is not the primary control centre for descending pain modulation. The dorsal horn of the spinal cord is a region in the spinal cord that receives and processes pain signals, but it is not a key structure in the descending pain modulation pathway. The nucleus raphe magnus is a region in the brainstem involved in the regulation of emotions and pain, but it is not the primary control centre for descending pain modulation. The reticular formation is a complex network of neurons in the brainstem involved in various functions, including arousal and attention, but it is not the primary control centre for descending pain modulation.

In summary, the periaqueductal gray is the primary control centre for descending pain modulation, and it plays a critical role in regulating pain signals in the body.

reference: Opposable thumb muscles -Emily can abduct (move away from midline) but not oppose (make close to midline) her thumb so opponens pollicis is damaged. -Flexor pollicis brevis and flexor digiti minimi brevis are both in the superficial layer of the anterior compartment of the hand and are responsible for flexion of the MCP joints. -Adductor pollicis is in the deep layer of the anterior compartment and is responsible for adduction (bring towards midline) of the thumb. -Abductor pollicis brevis is also in the superficial layer and is responsible for abduction (move away from midline) of the thumb. TIP-opposition vs abduction opposition=the ability to make close to midline in order to use the thumb as a thumb.abduction=the ability to move away from midline. eg if you put your thumb by your side and move it away from your side it's abduction. if you put your thumb by your side and move it closer to your thumb it's opposition.  reference https://teachmeanatomy.info/upper-limb/muscles/anterior-compartment/hand/opponens-pollicis/  and https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK537148/ Deltoid-A muscle located on the posterior side of the upper arm. It is one of the chief muscles of the rotator cuff. The deltoid is a large muscle with two heads (a superior and an inferior head) which are united by a common tendinous belly. The fibers of the deltoid are inserted into the tuberosity of the humerus.The main part of the deltoid muscle is located on the lateral border of the scapula above the teres minor. The deltoid is innervated by the axillary nerve and its main function is to provide stability to the glenohumeral joint and assist in abduction of the arm. Damage to this muscle may occur from a fractured humerus or dislocation of the shoulder. Nerve damage to the axillary nerve may cause weakness and paralysis of the deltoid.https://teachmeanatomy.info/upper-limb/muscles/posterior-compartment/deltoid/  and https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK537148/  LATERAL COLLATORAL LIGAMENT-a band of connective tissue that surrounds and supports the lateral condyle of the humerus. It is attached to the humeral shaft at one end and the greater tubercle of the humerus at the other. Its main part lies beneath the teres minor muscle, and its anterior and posterior margins lie respectively 3 and 3.5 cm lateral to the articular margin of the humeral shaft. The ligament prevents posterior displacement of the humeral head relative to the glenoid. This holds the humeral head tightly in the glenoid, thereby helping to stabilize the shoulder joint. A tear of this ligament is called a shoulder dislocation. A dislocation occurs when the force acting upon the glenohumeral joint is great enough to pull the humeral head from the glenoid. Dislocations generally occur in a forward direction; i.e., the humeral head is forced under the acromion process of the scapular. A dislocation can be reduced manually (by pressing the humeral head back into the glenoid), or surgery may be necessary. After a first-time dislocation, the glenohumeral joint is never truly "stable" again. The risk of future dislocations is always present. The supraspinatus is the most commonly torn muscle in the rotator cuff. It originates from the supraspinous fossa of the scapula above the teres minor and the great tubercle of the humerus. reference: Lignocaine (or lidocaine) is a amino amide local anaesthetic that inhibits fast-gated sodium channels. It is also used as an antiarrhythmic and as a stabiliser of the neuronal membrane. It is volatile and can be used with nitrous oxide as a vapour. Nitrous oxide is a weak vasodilator and lignocaine is a mild beta adrenoreceptor agonist so their interaction causes a slight decrease in blood pressure. Nitrous oxide has a very short half life and works quickly so is useful for minor surgery. The other options are all central nervous system depressants; diazepam is a benzodiazepine, propofol is a dissociative anaesthetic and amobarbital (also known as Amytal) is a barbiturate. These work by enhancing GABAergic activity. They have a high therapeutic index i.e. it takes a lot to overdose but they have a high risk of addiction and withdrawal symptoms. Nitrous oxide is very safe and has no major side effects or risks when used correctly.  All these drugs can be used as premedication before surgery. However, as fast-gated Na+ channels are also located in cardiac myocytes, the use of these drugs will also stop the heart. So unless there is an emergency, the above drugs cannot be used for this purpose.  I took most of this information from Dr Coffey's pharmacology light bulb. Amnesia can be caused by: - Certain medications - Trauma - Substance abuse - Infections such as herpes - Hypoxia/anoxia - Korsakoff Syndrome - Depression/schizophrenia - Head trauma - Stress - Alzheimer's disease - Stroke  Ageing is not a cause of amnesia, although memory loss is more common in older people due to age related decline in cognitive function. ==============================================================================================================  This was taken from the case 7 lecture on stroke and is a useful summary of different types of amnesia: There are different types of amnesia depending on what causes it. There are 2 main types: Anterograde – meaning memory loss that affects new memories. This is more common An example would be caused by head trauma or a strokeRetrograde – meaning memory loss that mainly affects old memories. This is less common Examples include; Korsakoff’s syndrome, alcoholic memory loss, herpes simplex virus infection, hypothyroidism, depression, schizophrenia, alzheimers  Another type is temporary amnesia which can be caused by; trauma, stress, seizures, severe emotional distress, oxygen deprivation, ingestion of certain drugs, alcohol withdrawal, sleep disorders, hyperventilation, head injury, hypoglycemia, hyperthyroidism  All these different causes have one thing in common – they cause disruption to short term memory. Memory loss can be either retrograde (prior to illness/injury) or anterograde (after illness/injury). Sometimes there is a reversible cause e.g. vitamin B12 deficiency, thiamine deficiency, hypercalcemia. Sometimes it is irreversible e.g. anoxia/hypoxia, traumatic brain injury, bleeding into the brain/around the brain.  People often confuse dementia with amnesia but they are not the same thing. Dementia is a broader term that describes a decline in cognitive function that is so severe it interferes with daily life. Memory loss is just one symptom of dementia. For example someone may have vascular dementia where they have had a series of mini-strokes which causes memory loss but they may still remember things from before their illness. Whereas with Korsakoff syndrome the patient will have difficulty recalling both recent and past memories.  Case 6 lecture on semantic dementia highlighted how memory loss can be profound yet the person is often aware of this and finds it very distressing. They may know what they want to say but the words aren’t there. It is thought that semantic dementia may be the most common form of early onset dementia. During the early stages of development before the placenta forms, it is the developing embryo that produces hCG. This is because the mother's immune system does not yet recognise the developing foetus as a 'self' cell. Instead, it recognises the embryo as a foreign object and would attempt to destroy it. Leydig cells are found in the testicles and are responsible for producing testosterone. If a male has low levels of testosterone, hCG can be administered to stimulate the production of Leydig cells which will then produce testosterone. input: Given question: You are shadowing an eye surgeon and he suddenly turns to you and asks, 'WHAT TYPE OF COLLAGEN IS FOUND IN THE CORNEA!!!!'. You are caught off-guard and can't quite remember what type. What type of collagen is found in the cornea? Option A: Type I Option B: Type II Option C: Type III Option D: Type IV Option E: Type V The correct answer is Option A.
reference:
The cornea is made up of Type I collagen. This is the same as scar tissue and bone. It is a structural collagen. There are 3 main layers to the cornea - epithelium, Bowman's membrane (Type IV collagen) and stroma (Type I collagen). The stroma is the thickest layer and is made almost entirely of Type I collagen. This gives the cornea it's strength. In addition, there are also nerve endings, blood vessels and macrophages present in the stroma. The cornea has a very high oxygen concentration which is important in preventing infection by reducing the numbers of microorganisms that can survive. The cornea also contains some keratan sulfate and chondroitin sulfate. These give the cornea additional strength and help to prevent dehydration. The epithelium is composed of multiple layers of cells which are held together by desmosine and laminine. The most important cell in the epithelium is the corneal keratocyte. It is believed that these cells are responsible for creating new corneas in case of damage. Finally, the Bowman's membrane is a thin layer of collagen that separates the cornea from the sclera. It is named after its discoverer, Sir William Bowman. It is thought that this layer may help to even out any irregularities in the surface of the cornea so that the light is not distorted as it enters the eye.
